summary: Describes the H ratio, a measure of how efficiently an address space is used when assigning addresses. It was submitted to the IPng effort to help judge address-assignment schemes. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A score telling how much of a big pile of numbered mailboxes is really being used.

questions: is 128 bits enough for ipv6 addresses
subtitle: A logarithmic yardstick for how efficiently an address space is actually used.

tldr.problem: During the IPng debate people judged address plans by 'assignment efficiency', but the simple ratio of systems to possible addresses is misleading because addresses are hierarchical.
tldr.mechanism: The memo proposes H = log(number of objects) divided by available bits, with base 10 logs, which varies between 0 and 0.30103.
tldr.outcome: Real numbering plans show H usually between 0.14 and 0.26, and the author concludes that 128 bits is more than enough.

today: RFC 1715 is an Informational memo that is updated by RFC 3194.

sections.title: Efficiency of Address Assignment
sections.content:
The memo was submitted to the IETF IPng area in response to RFC 1550. Publication does not imply acceptance by the IPng area of any ideas in it.

People in the IPng debate expressed assignment efficiency as the effective number of systems over the theoretical maximum. On that measure, 32-bit IP addressing, with about 3.5 millions of addresses reported in the DNS, gives 0.05%. The author calls this classic evaluation misleading because it ignores the hierarchy of network, subnet and host.
sections.eli5: Counting filled seats in a theatre is not fair when seats are grouped in rows and sections. A fairer score is needed.

sections.title: The H Ratio
sections.content:
The proposal is H = log(number of objects) / available bits. Because it is logarithmic, it depends little on the number of hierarchical levels: two levels of 8 bits with 100 elements each give the same result as one level of 16 bits with 10000 elements.

The memo uses base 10 logs, so H varies between 0 and a theoretical maximum of 0.30103, the log base 10 of 2.
sections.eli5: The score counts digits of how many things you have, divided by digits of room available. Splitting the room into levels does not change it.

sections.title: Values Seen in Practice
sections.content:
The author looks at the moment when numbering plans broke and had to grow. Examples include French telephone numbers (0.26), the US telephone system (about 0.24), the Internet at about 3 million hosts (0.20, rising to 0.23 with ten times more hosts), SITA addresses (0.14), the physics/space science DECnet Phase IV (0.26) and about 200 million IEEE 802 nodes (0.18).

From these the memo asserts that the efficiency ratio usually lies between 0.14 and 0.26.
sections.eli5: He checks old phone and computer networks at the moment they ran out of room, and sees they were all about equally full.

sections.title: Evaluating Address Plans
sections.content:
Working in reverse gives population counts for each address size at the pessimistic (0.14) and optimistic (0.26) ratios. For 32 bits that is 3 E+4 to 2 E+8; for 128 bits it is 8 E+17 to 2 E+33.

The author says this explains why some feel 64 bits is 'not enough' while others call it sufficient, and concludes 128 bits is 'more than enough', since even the lowest efficiency is above the hyperbolic estimate of 1.E+15 Internet hosts. The memo says security issues are not discussed.
sections.eli5: Depending on how full you expect addresses to be, a medium-sized address might be too small or plenty. The biggest size is safe either way.
